title: Common-Mode Response
intro: Real differential pairs are not perfectly symmetric and their tail is not an ideal current source. Both let a change in the input common-mode level leak to the output.

blocks.text: Let the tail have output resistance $R_{SS}$ and drive both gates with $V_{in,CM}$. By symmetry X and Y move together, so they can be shorted, and M1 and M2, now sharing all terminals, merge into one device with twice the width, twice the current and $2g_m$. The circuit is a degenerated CS stage with load $R_D/2$:

blocks.alt: Left: differential pair with both gates at V in CM and a tail resistor RSS. Right: equivalent circuit, a single transistor M1 plus M2 with transconductance 2gm, load RD over 2, and source resistor RSS.
blocks.caption: With a common-mode input the symmetric pair folds into one double-width transistor.

blocks.text: In a symmetric circuit this CM gain does not corrupt the differential output, but it moves the bias point: the output CM level shifts, which eats into headroom and can push the input devices towards triode. In nanometer processes the tail's output resistance is low, so a CM change at the first stage shifts its output CM, which shifts the next stage, and so on.

The serious problem appears when the two halves differ. With load mismatch $R_{D2} = R_D + \Delta R_D$, the merged input devices act as a source follower that raises P by $\frac{R_{SS}}{R_{SS} + 1/(2g_m)}\Delta V_{in,CM}$, so each drain current rises by the same $\frac{g_m}{1 + 2g_m R_{SS}}\Delta V_{in,CM}$, but the two outputs move by different amounts:

blocks.tex: \Delta V_X - \Delta V_Y = \frac{g_m\,\Delta R_D}{1 + 2 g_m R_{SS}}\,\Delta V_{in,CM}

blocks.text: A CM disturbance now produces a differential error that is indistinguishable from signal. Input-transistor mismatch (size and $V_{TH}$) is usually a larger source than resistor mismatch. With transconductances $g_{m1} \ne g_{m2}$, node P follows the input as $V_P = \frac{(g_{m1} + g_{m2})R_{SS}}{1 + (g_{m1} + g_{m2})R_{SS}}V_{in,CM}$, the drain currents are $g_{m1,2}(V_{in,CM} - V_P)$, and the differential output gives the conversion gain

blocks.tex: A_{CM-DM} = -\frac{\Delta g_m R_D}{1 + (g_{m1} + g_{m2}) R_{SS}}, \qquad \Delta g_m = g_{m1} - g_{m2}

blocks.text: The tail node always carries capacitance (the tail device's own drain capacitance plus the source-bulk junctions of M1 and M2). Replacing $R_{SS}$ by the impedance of that capacitance $C_P$ shows that even a perfect current source cannot stop CM-to-DM conversion at high frequency:
A typical case is supply noise reaching the drains of a first stage and from there the gates of a second pair: the error grows with the noise frequency.
To compare circuits fairly, the unwanted CM-to-DM gain is normalised to the wanted differential gain:
Taking only a $g_m$ mismatch, the differential gain with mismatched devices and the resulting CMRR are

blocks.tex: |A_{DM}| = \frac{R_D}{2}\cdot\frac{g_{m1} + g_{m2} + 4 g_{m1} g_{m2} R_{SS}}{1 + (g_{m1} + g_{m2}) R_{SS}}, \qquad \mathrm{CMRR} = \frac{g_{m1} + g_{m2} + 4 g_{m1} g_{m2} R_{SS}}{2\Delta g_m}
\mathrm{CMRR} \approx \frac{g_m}{\Delta g_m}(1 + 2 g_m R_{SS}) \approx \frac{2 g_m^2 R_{SS}}{\Delta g_m}
blocks.caption: $g_m$ is the mean of $g_{m1}$ and $g_{m2}$; the last form holds when $2g_m R_{SS} \gg 1$.

blocks.text: CMRR is set by matching and tail impedance together. Better layout matching and a higher-impedance tail (longer or cascoded) both help, and the tail capacitance limits CMRR at high frequency no matter how good the DC tail is.

An ideal tail does not guarantee infinite CMRR either: a CM change moves node P and hence $V_{BS}$ of both input devices, and if their body-effect transconductances differ ($g_{mb1} \ne g_{mb2}$) the drain currents change by different amounts.

blocks.title: CMRR estimate
blocks.text: $g_m = 2\text{ mS}$, $R_{SS} = 20\text{ k}\Omega$, and a 1 percent mismatch $\Delta g_m/g_m$. Find the CMRR in dB.

blocks.title: Effect of the tail
blocks.text: If $R_{SS}$ is raised from 20 kΩ to 200 kΩ with the same $g_m$ and mismatch, what is the new CMRR?
solution: A tenfold larger tail resistance gives about a tenfold better CMRR, 20 dB more.

blocks.title: Common-mode shift with a resistor tail
blocks.text: A pair uses a resistor tail that drops 0.4 V at 0.8 mA. $\mu_n C_{ox} W/L = 5\text{ mA/V}^2$, $V_{TH} = 0.45\text{ V}$, $V_{DD} = 1.8\text{ V}$. (a) What input CM level is needed? (b) Choose $R_D$ for a differential gain of 4 and find how far the inputs are from triode. (c) What happens if the input CM rises by 50 mV?
blocks.hint: Use the merged-transistor equivalent for the CM change.
solution: (a) Each side carries 0.4 mA, so $V_{ov} = \sqrt{2 \cdot 0.4/5} = 0.4\text{ V}$, $V_{GS} = 0.85\text{ V}$ and $V_{in,CM} = 0.85 + 0.4 = 1.25\text{ V}$. The tail resistor is $R_{SS} = 0.4/0.8\text{ mA} = 500\text{ }\Omega$.

(b) $g_m = 2I_D/V_{ov} = 2\text{ mS}$, so $R_D = 4/g_m = 2\text{ k}\Omega$. The outputs sit at $1.8 - 0.4\text{ mA} \cdot 2\text{ k}\Omega = 1.0\text{ V}$; triode starts when the drain falls to $V_{in,CM} - V_{TH} = 0.8\text{ V}$, a margin of 0.2 V.

(c) The outputs fall by $50\text{ mV} \cdot \frac{R_D/2}{R_{SS} + 1/(2g_m)} = 50 \cdot \frac{1000}{750} = 66.7\text{ mV}$, while the gate rises 50 mV. The margin shrinks to $0.2 - 0.05 - 0.067 = 0.083\text{ V}$.
blocks.answer: (a) 1.25 V; (b) 2 kΩ with 0.2 V margin; (c) margin drops to about 83 mV.

blocks.title: Conversion at high frequency
blocks.text: A pair with an ideal tail has $g_{m1} + g_{m2} = 4\text{ mS}$, $\Delta g_m = 0.04\text{ mS}$ (1 percent), $R_D = 5\text{ k}\Omega$ and 200 fF at the tail node. Find $|A_{CM-DM}|$ at 100 MHz and 1 GHz.
blocks.hint: $\Delta g_m R_D = 0.2$ is the conversion gain with no tail at all.
solution: At 100 MHz, $C_P\omega = 200\text{ fF} \cdot 2\pi \cdot 10^8 = 0.126\text{ mS}$, so $(g_{m1} + g_{m2})/(C_P\omega) = 31.8$ and $|A_{CM-DM}| = 0.2/\sqrt{1 + 31.8^2} = 0.0063$.
At 1 GHz the ratio is 3.18, giving $0.2/\sqrt{1 + 10.1} = 0.060$, about ten times worse.
blocks.answer: About 0.006 at 100 MHz and 0.06 at 1 GHz.
